Keywords: Hermes, Writing, Spider

outputs.L1:
It is Hermes stepping out of his winged sandal.  
Even his caduceus—despite the scandal  
of its forfeiture—lies abandoned,  
like an Android or iPad on a nightstand  
grown footed for the purpose of bearing away  
any such device or gadget as may  
distract him from a more pressing matter.  
Herse is perched on the precipice of the mattress  
with its luxurious bedspread, where tapestry,  
vis-à-vis itself, interleaves the allegory.  
Real gold thread weighs upon the covers  
a cherub heaves to turn down for the lovers.  
Would that the same, in his wings, might tip the scales  
and, with tears, put salt into these mythical tales  
by sinking level with us—l’enfant in the room....

I saw the Writing Spider sitting with aplomb,  
dead center in her creation, above the compost  
(a sage location). What I wondered most  
was whether the sweetgum burrs and dried leaves  
were ornaments or accidents she interweaves  
in the clearly golden silk, whose subwebs  
are occupied by diminutive male sub-celebs,  
holding down the fort—as she holds court—  
long after she vanishes, stopping short  
of the epiphany or apotheosis  
we expect from genteel arts, or a goddess:

“Who thereupon did rende the cloth in pieces every whit,  
Bicause the lewdnesse of the Gods was biased so in it.  
And with an Arras weavers combe of Box she fiercely smit  
Arachne on the forehead full a dozen times and more.”
outputs.L2:
Hermes is stepping out of his winged footwear. Even his caduceus has been cast aside—scandalous though that surrender may be—like a tablet or Android device left on a bedside table equipped with feet, ready to carry off any gadget that could divert him from something more urgent.

Meanwhile, I observed the Writing Spider poised confidently at the exact center of her web, suspended over the compost heap—a judicious choice of setting. What intrigued me most was whether the sweetgum pods and brittle leaves woven into the unmistakably golden strands were intentional decorations or mere chance additions. Smaller webs housed tiny, lesser-known males who continued guarding the structure, just as she presided over it, long after she had disappeared. Yet the scene never quite achieved the revelation or divine transformation one might anticipate from refined art—or from a goddess.

Herse balances at the very edge of the bed, which is covered by an opulent spread. In its woven design, the tapestry folds its allegory back upon itself. Genuine gold filament makes the covering so heavy that a cherub must strain to draw it down for the lovers. If only that same weight could burden Hermes’ wings, shift the balance, and season these legendary stories with tears by bringing the child in the room down to our mortal level.

Then she ripped the entire fabric into shreds because it portrayed the gods’ debauchery, and, using a boxwood comb belonging to an Arras weaver, struck Arachne squarely on the forehead at least twelve times.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by observing a writing spider poised at the center of her golden web. The web is not an isolated work of natural perfection: it gathers the materials of the surrounding world, incorporating leaves, prickly sweetgum burrs, and even the bodies of tiny male spiders. This mixture of beauty, debris, and violence establishes the poem’s interest in art as something both intricate and unsettling.

The scene then shifts into mythology. Hermes seems to have cast aside his winged sandal and caduceus as casually as a modern person might abandon distracting gadgets. He is absorbed instead by a more urgent romantic pursuit. Herse, the object of his desire, waits on an opulent bed covered with richly woven fabrics. The bedcovers become more than decoration: their elaborate designs blur the boundary between physical tapestry and mythological allegory, turning the setting itself into a work of art that tells—or conceals—a story.

Throughout the poem, idealized divine art is placed beside ordinary earthly details. This contrast raises questions about the purpose of ornament and artistic representation. Do beautiful patterns reveal deeper truths, or do they merely distract the viewer with surface splendor? The poem suggests that art can perform both functions: it can seduce and obscure, but it can also expose what power would prefer to keep hidden.

This tension is embodied most dramatically in the story of Arachne. Her tapestry depicts the gods not as noble and perfect beings, but as figures guilty of deception, sexual violence, and other immoral acts. Because her art reveals these divine scandals so clearly, she is violently punished. Arachne’s fate shows that the danger of art lies not simply in its beauty or technical brilliance, but in its capacity to tell uncomfortable truths about those who hold power.
outputs.L4:
The text brings together mythology, art, technology, and divine scandal through a series of vivid, interconnected images. At its center is Arachne’s web: both a woven object and a form of storytelling capable of recording what official versions of myth would prefer to conceal. The web becomes a technology of representation, transforming thread into testimony and artistic skill into a means of confronting power.

Alongside Arachne’s tapestry appear the abandoned accessories of Hermes and the intimate setting of Herse’s bed. These objects strip the gods of their ceremonial grandeur. Hermes is no longer merely an immaculate divine messenger; the traces he leaves behind suggest desire, disorder, and compromised dignity. Herse’s bed likewise brings mythology into a private, bodily realm, where divine actions can be seen not as lofty symbols but as acts shaped by lust, deception, and vulnerability.

A quoted account of Arachne’s punishment intensifies this conflict between artistic truth and divine authority. Arachne is punished not simply because she possesses extraordinary technical skill, but because she uses that skill to expose the gods’ sexual misconduct and hypocrisy. Her weaving challenges the idealized image that divine power creates for itself. By depicting scandalous episodes with precision and beauty, she demonstrates that art can preserve truths that authority would rather suppress.

Weaving therefore functions as more than a traditional craft. It becomes a model for narration itself: separate strands are joined, images are arranged, and hidden relationships are made visible. The artist and the storyteller both construct patterns that allow viewers or readers to recognize the flaws beneath heroic or sacred appearances. In this sense, technology is not opposed to art. The loom is a tool, but it is also a medium of memory, criticism, and revelation.

The text ultimately brings myth down to a distinctly human level. Its gods are not remote embodiments of perfection; they are jealous, lecherous, vindictive, and anxious about challenges to their authority. Arachne’s fate reveals how power responds when art refuses to flatter it. Although she is defeated and transformed, the truth contained in her work survives through the story of her punishment. The web thus stands as an enduring symbol of art’s capacity to expose scandal, question idealized authority, and turn even divine imperfection into a subject for human judgment.
outputs.L5:
Hermes sat beneath an olive tree, writing messages for the gods. His pen moved quickly, but not as quickly as the small spider spinning a web between two branches above him.

He watched the delicate threads cross and connect, forming a pattern that seemed almost like an alphabet.

“You write without ink,” Hermes said.

“And you weave without silk,” replied the spider.

Hermes smiled. He understood then that writing was another kind of web: each word a thread, each sentence a careful connection. A message could travel farther than its author, catching thoughts, memories, and hearts along the way.

Before leaving, Hermes placed his unfinished page beside the web. By morning, the spider had woven a single silver thread across it—nature’s signature beneath the words of a god.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental ekphrastic poem that interweaves a Writing Spider in its web with a classical tapestry depicting Hermes and Herse, incorporating modern devices, mythological imagery, and a quotation about Arachne.
counterfactuals.output:
### **ARGIOPE, OR THE GOD IN AIRPLANE MODE**

In the museum’s blue-lit hush  
a Writing Spider edits the corner—

eight black styluses,  
abdomen dipped in warning-yellow,  
her web’s white zigzag  
a sentence struck by lightning:

                         X  
                    X         X  
               X       *         X

Behind her, the tapestry keeps buffering:

**HERMES DESCENDING TO ATHENS**,  
winged sandals pixelated with gold thread,  
caduceus twined like a charging cable,  
his cloud a pale notification  
no mortal has consented to receive.

Herse walks among the Panathenaic girls,  
bearing wool / bearing silence /  
bearing her face in profile  
as if the loom had invented beauty  
and could not undo it.

Hermes sees her.

The god’s heart clicks  
**ALLOW LOCATION ACCESS?**

                         YES  
                         ALWAYS  
                         WHILE USING DESIRE

The spider types across the air.

Her alphabet is hunger.  
Her punctuation: flies wrapped  
in small white shrouds.  
Her signature flashes ultraviolet—  
a QR code addressed to the sun.

In the woven doorway, Aglaurus  
becomes envy, becomes firewall,  
becomes stone one green byte at a time.  
Mercury lifts his wand.  
The threads tighten around her knees.

Someone’s phone photographs the scene  
and mistakes the spider for damage.

Zoom in:

each strand is a road from Olympus,  
each knot a little mortal refusal.  
Hermes is forever almost arriving;  
Herse is forever made of elsewhere.  
The shuttle passes left to right,  
right to left—

a god refreshed,  
a girl archived.

> “Arachne, though, no longer human, still  
> continued spinning.”  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses*

So the label says. So the web revises.

Not punishment, writes Argiope,  
but practice.

Not metamorphosis,  
but the body learning  
its correct technology.

She hangs head-down before the tapestry,  
a dark cursor blinking over myth,  
and drags one silver filament  
from Hermes’ open mouth  
to Herse’s unanswering hand.

The gallery Wi-Fi fails.

Winged messages fall from the ceiling.  
Cloud storage opens into weather.  
Every screen goes black enough  
to show its watcher.

Only the spider remains online,

uploading the ancient image  
into the live, trembling server of her web—

god / girl / stone / loom,  
desire caught in its own design—

and at the center,  
where no human sentence can hold,

a bright unwoven X:

                         SEND  
                         SEND  
                         SEND
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal collage poem comparing spiderweb construction to tapestry weaving, blending observations of sweetgum burrs and dried leaves with the myths of Hermes, Herse, and Arachne. Let the syntax visually and semantically interleave as though two poems were superimposed.
counterfactuals.output:
### **LOOM / ORB**

Hermes threads the morning                 the spider measures air  
with a gold, wing-footed shuttle—          leg over leg, a dark refrain,  
toward Herse at her window,                fastening nothing to nothing  
dew-daughter, sister of rain.              until nothing can bear weight.

        Between them:  
a sweetgum burr, fallen planet,  
hooks its hundred wooden mouths  
into the hem of a dried oak leaf—  
                                     *stay / tear / stay.*

He brings no fleece but rumor;             she brings no wool but hunger.  
The doorway hardens—Aglauros, stone—        the branch bends, an antlered loom.  
His wand parts sleep from sleep             her silk divides the vacant blue:  
                warp: desire                        weft: weather  
                warp: god                           weft: fly  
                warp: Herse                         weft: absence.

Arachne, beneath the bark,  
                        above Olympus,  
                inside the spider’s abdomen,  
ties truth to truth so finely  
Athena calls it insolence.

The tapestry says: **gods enter rooms as gold.**  
The web says:                 **all gold is adhesive.**  
The tapestry says: **Herse opened like daylight.**  
The web says:                 **daylight is full of wings.**

Dried leaves applaud in their ruined hands,  
brown palms rubbing                         /rubbing/  
                        the season thin.

Sweetgum burrs roll under Hermes’ sandals—  
small spiked looms, snarled suns,  
each one weaving the dust  
                             without thread.

And now the two makers cross:

Arachne casts her shuttle     ╲         the spider casts herself  
                                 ╲  
Hermes becomes a silver strand  ╳     Herse becomes the dew  
                                 ╱  
a leaf tears free               ╱        a moth does not.

By dusk, the web is a tapestry  
of what escaped and what did not;  
the tapestry, a web  
in which every pictured god is caught.

         At the center—

                 no queen,  
         no fly,  
                 no answer—

only a burr wearing one dead leaf  
like a crown of torn bronze,

and Arachne’s eight-fold signature  
stitched across the wind:

             **enter             be taken**  
             **love              be stone**  
             **weave             be woven.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an avant-garde ekphrasis of a Renaissance tapestry showing Hermes visiting Herse, juxtaposed against a Writing Spider sitting at the center of her golden web. Use puns, parenthetical asides, disrupted line breaks, and a passage from an old English translation of the Arachne story.
counterfactuals.output:
### **WOVEN MESSAGE, OR: MERCURY IN THE MARGINS**

The tapestry begins by refusing  
to begin—

gold thread stuttering at the border,  
a little sun undone into bullion syllables.

There: Hermes, all wing-tip and afterthought,  
descends toward Herse’s chamber  
with his caduceus tuned to a double meaning:  
*commerce / come-hither*,  
the snakes negotiating every knot.

He has dressed as weather.  
He has dressed as a sentence arriving too quickly.  
His helmet says **elsewhere**,  
his sandals say

                              now.

Herse—dew-girl, hear-say, her-silk—  
stands among the maidens of Athens,  
white arms lifted beneath the loom’s arrested thunder.  
Her body is a pale grammatical case  
Mercury means to decline.

(Behind the door, Aglauros counts envy  
coin by green coin.)

Yet at the tapestry’s exact  
unquiet center—

not Hermes, not Herse, not even the god’s  
golden offer—

a Writing Spider sits in her aureate web:  
Argiope, argot-pe,  
eight-legged amanuensis  
with an abdomen inked like a small heraldic mask.

She has written one dazzling zigzag  
down the page of air:

              Z  
                I  
              G  
                Z  
              A  
                G—

a stabilimentum, scholars call it,  
though nothing is stable here.

The web catches light.  
The light catches Hermes.  
Hermes, suddenly the message rather than the messenger,  
hangs in the shining syntax  
of his own desire.

*“Among the Lydians dwelt a maid, Arachne was hir name,  
Who in the cunning skill of worke had won hirselfe such fame…”*

—Ovid, *Metamorphoses*,  
in Arthur Golding’s old English translation, 1567.

The quotation frays.  
The letters crawl back into legs.

Arachne / Argiope:  
two artisans sharing one punishing signature.  
One challenged heaven with wool;  
one punctuates heaven daily  
and eats whatever misreads her.

Look closely: the Renaissance weavers have couched  
a second story beneath the first.  
Hermes’s cloak is feathered with flies.  
Herse’s golden girdle becomes a radial line.  
The palace columns bend into anchor threads.  
Even Athena’s absent eye  
glitters in the spider’s thorax—

(needle knows needle).

And what is love here  
but a tactful entanglement?  
What is tapestry but a wall taught to remember  
its wounds?

Hermes raises the wand.

The spider does not move.

He offers language, exchange,  
a purse fat with mortal permissions.

She answers in web-work:

                         writ  
                         writhe  
                         write—

Herse reaches toward him, perhaps.  
Or toward the spider.  
Or toward the severed margin  
where the scene’s gold ground has begun  
to molt.

No mouth opens.  
Every thread is speaking.

Above them, the woven sky puckers  
like fabric held too near a flame;  
below, flowers flatten themselves into emblems,  
each petal a parenthesis  
(containing its own little fall).

The god remains forever visiting.  
The girl remains forever almost visited.  
The spider, meanwhile, completes her bright correction:

a cross-stitch through Mercury’s chest,  
a flourish under Herse’s name,

and at the center of the center  
places her body—

black comma,  
gold question,

the living mark from which  
no story  
can safely  
fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, nonlinear poem about weaving, art, scandal, and divine desire. Merge a garden spider’s web with an ornate mythological bedchamber, mention diminutive males, abandoned gadgets, “l’enfant in the room,” and end with imagery of tears salting classical myths.
counterfactuals.output:
A garden spider sutures dusk to the balustrade—  
orb after orb, a pearl geometry hung  
across the ornate mythological bedchamber,  
where swans molt in the coverlet, gold rains  
through the locked ceiling, and every carved nymph  
turns her scandalous face toward the loom.

Diminutive males tremble at the silk’s margin,  
brief commas in her sumptuous theorem;  
desire, divine and cannibal, perfumes the columns.  
Under the bed: abandoned gadgets—  
a cracked lyre, a dead phone, Hermes’ obsolete wing—  
still blinking rumors into the dust.

Arachne works backward. Athena sleeps forward.  
Between them, l’enfant in the room  
draws one red thread through the family resemblance:  
art as trap, worship as appetite, beauty  
the bruise gossip leaves on the immortal body.

Who entered whom—the web, the chamber,  
the god disguised as weather? Curtains billow  
with unsworn testimony. Mirrors embroider  
another mirror. At dawn the spider eats  
the evidence, yet the bed keeps shining,  
its posts crowded with violated constellations—

and from the torn canopy fall slow tears,  
salting Europa, Leda, Danaë,  
salting all the classical myths.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
